beats.narration_text: Tools like SurveyMind generate synthetic survey respondents — AI personas standing in for real humans so researchers can skip recruiting. Fine, if the personas actually think like people. But nothing stops a model from generating Big Five scores that look plausible trait by trait while the relationships BETWEEN traits — the actual structure of a human personality — are quietly wrong. Ship that into a study and every downstream finding is built on a correlation matrix that was never real. SurveyMind's own paper admits this validation hasn't been run yet. So we built the test.

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat — the ACTUAL generated code, trimmed to what teaches
beats.narration_text: Read it before trusting it. The congruence coefficient is Tucker's phi — cosine similarity between the two matrices' unique correlations, upper triangle only, so we're not double-counting. Above point-nine, the structures agree. The Jennrich test asks the sharper question: are these two matrices statistically distinguishable at all, not just visually close. And the bootstrap resamples the smaller, synthetic set two thousand times so the confidence interval isn't a lie built on one lucky draw.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

def tucker_congruence(r1, r2):
    iu = np.triu_indices_from(r1, k=1)
    v1, v2 = r1[iu], r2[iu]
    return np.sum(v1 * v2) / np.sqrt(np.sum(v1**2) * np.sum(v2**2))

beats.narration_text: Real SurveyMind output isn't public yet, so first we stress-test the validator itself: a synthetic set we built by hand to match the real human structure. Congruence coefficient: point-nine-eight — the correlation structures line up. The Jennrich test can't reject that they're the same matrix. This is what a PASS looks like when the pipeline works correctly — not a claim about SurveyMind itself yet.

beats.narration_text: A validator that only ever says pass isn't a validator. Check it: point it at a synthetic set we deliberately broke and see if it catches the fake. Into Claude: re-run pipeline dot py against a synthetic sample with a distorted trait relationship and report every gate.

props.command:
claude "re-run pipeline.py against a synthetic sample with
distorted Neuroticism relationships —
report congruence, Jennrich, bootstrap CI, and per-trait KS for every gate"

beats.role_note: REAL SCREEN RECORDING REQUIRED. Not fillable by me — you need to record your own terminal running pipeline.py on the distorted scenario and drop it in as media/B06.mp4. Real numbers to expect on screen: congruence 0.5946, Jennrich p<0.0001.
beats.narration_text: Same script, same real human data, now against a synthetic set with its Neuroticism relationships deliberately flattened. Congruence coefficient drops to point-five-nine. The Jennrich test rejects: these matrices are statistically different, not a rounding error. Bootstrap CI no longer touches point-nine. And two of the five traits fail their KS test outright. The validator catches exactly what it's supposed to catch — a synthetic respondent that looks fine trait by trait but got the relationships between traits wrong.
beats.visual_intent: same screen-recording layout as B04, now showing the deliberately-broken run — lower congruence number highlighted, Jennrich significant result in red, bootstrap CI shifted down, KS table with flagged rows, ending on a red FAIL

beats.role_note: the lesson — one beat, honest about scope. FIXED: was an unfilled gen-AI slate; using FormACard house-style card instead.
beats.narration_text: So the risk was never whether synthetic scores look plausible — they always do. It's whether the correlations between traits match a real human personality's structure. Congruence coefficient, Jennrich, bootstrap, and per-trait KS together catch what eyeballing a distribution never will. What we've proven here is that the test works: real human data in one hand, a synthetic set in the other, and a pipeline that correctly tells them apart when they should be told apart. The actual verdict on SurveyMind itself is still pending real data.
